text: Were international relations governed purely by self-interest, cooperation between nations would rarely, if ever, occur. Yet history demonstrates that even fierce rivals can be persuaded to negotiate when the alternative — allowing a conflict to escalate unchecked — proves too costly. Diplomacy remains the primary mechanism through which sovereign states resolve disputes without resorting to force. A skilled envoy, for instance, can mediate between hostile parties, laying the groundwork for a ceasefire that might otherwise seem unattainable. Not only do bilateral talks build trust between two nations, but broader coalitions and alliances also create the collective leverage needed to enforce sanctions against those who violate international norms. Nevertheless, tensions inevitably arise when one nation acts unilaterally, disregarding the autonomy or sovereignty of its neighbors in pursuit of regional hegemony. Such actions can undermine painstakingly negotiated treaties and complicate the delicate process of reconciliation. Geopolitical rivalries, moreover, rarely resolve themselves; they require sustained deterrence alongside genuine willingness to compromise. Only when nations ratify agreements in good faith — rather than treating them as mere formalities — can lasting peace be achieved. In this sense, diplomacy is not weakness but perhaps the most demanding form of strength a nation can exercise.
